lesson.title: The Common Tongue of Networked Programs: The Berkeley Sockets API
lesson.summary: The Berkeley sockets API is the foundational programming interface, originating in early 1980s BSD Unix, that represents a network connection as a socket and underlies essentially every modern operating system's networking support.
lesson.body:
Almost every piece of software that talks over a network, from a web browser to a game server, is ultimately built on top of the Berkeley sockets API. It originated at UC Berkeley in the early 1980s as part of BSD Unix, and its design proved influential enough that essentially every modern operating system offers a socket interface modeled on it, Linux, macOS, and Windows through its Winsock implementation among them, even though the fine details differ from platform to platform.

The central idea is the socket itself: a handle representing one end of a communication channel, conceptually similar to a file descriptor used for reading and writing files. Once a program has created a socket, it can send and receive data through it using a fairly small, consistent set of function calls, without needing to hand craft packets or manage the lower level details of how bytes actually get moved across the network. That consistency is exactly what makes it practical to write networked software at all.

This also clarifies where the sockets API sits relative to the application layer. Applications live above the transport layer, and the sockets API is the boundary between the two: it is the set of calls an application uses to ask the operating system's networking stack to send or receive data on its behalf. Application layer protocols, such as HTTP, are themselves implemented using these same socket calls underneath.

A handful of core operations make up the backbone of this API, and each gets its own dedicated chapter ahead. socket() creates a socket of a chosen type, SOCK_STREAM for TCP or SOCK_DGRAM for UDP. bind() attaches a local address to a socket. On the TCP side, listen() and accept() prepare a socket to receive incoming connections from the server's perspective, while connect() is what a client uses to establish an outbound connection. On the UDP side, there is no connection to set up at all, so sendto() and recvfrom() carry data along with an explicit address on every single call instead.

It is worth pausing on why one API comfortably covers both TCP and UDP. The socket abstraction separates the question of what a communication endpoint is from the question of how reliably the underlying protocol delivers data. That separation is what lets the same conceptual model, and largely the same set of function calls, support both a reliable ordered byte stream and a lightweight, unreliable datagram service, with the differences showing up mainly in which specific calls a program needs to use.
